script.opening: (Gruff, a bit breathless between phrases but speaking in full sentences; cigarette packet visible on the table.) "Morning doc. It's my chest again — I'm more puffed than usual, coughing more, and the phlegm's gone green. I know the drill, I just need my steroids and antibiotics like last time. And please don't start on about the smoking, I've heard it all before."

facts.text: "Four days. Worse walking. I'm alright sitting." Can walk to the kitchen but not the shops. Talking in full sentences.
"Loads more. Thick and green" — usually a bit of white in the mornings.

Fever: "No." Chest pain on breathing in, sudden onset, calf swelling: "None of that." "No blood. Not that I've noticed with the weight." Swollen ankles or needing more pillows: "No, no." Not confused or drowsy. Has no home oximeter.

Diagnosed 6 years ago. Two rescue courses last year, no admissions. Last spirometry: FEV1 about 45%. Uses tiotropium/olodaterol inhaler daily and salbutamol — using salbutamol 6–8 times a day now. Previous sputum sample: none sent. Has had flu and pneumococcal jabs; not sure about COVID booster.
Inhalers only. No allergies (has had amoxicillin and doxycycline before without problems).

20 a day since 15 — about 40 pack-years. Tried to stop twice with patches, lasted a fortnight each time. If asked permission to discuss it: "Go on. You will anyway." Then: "It's too late now. And it's the only thing I enjoy."
Retired bus driver. Lives with his wife, Pat, who smokes outside. Two grandchildren he looks after on Fridays. Drinks 2 pints on a Saturday.

Defensive, keen to get the prescription. Relaxes if the doctor deals with his chest properly first. If lectured about smoking, shut down: "Told you." If the doctor asks permission and makes a brief, respectful offer, accept a referral grudgingly: "Send them. No promises." Will come in today if needed: "I can pop in."

ice.ideas: "Same as always. My chest. It's what happens."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — guilt and fatalism about smoking ("too late now"); tired of being lectured; quietly worried about not being around for his grandchildren.
ice.expectations: "Just want it sorted. And not the lecture."

cues: "Don't start on about the smoking." — defensiveness; ask permission later.
"It's too late now." — fatalism to gently challenge.
"The only thing I enjoy." — what smoking means to him.

checkpoints.text: Assesses exacerbation SEVERITY (breathlessness at rest/sentences, sats if he has a home oximeter, accessory muscles, confusion/cyanosis — with a same-day face-to-face assessment if in doubt, as he cannot be examined by video) and EXCLUDES alternative causes — pneumonia (fever), PE (pleuritic pain/calf), heart failure (orthopnoea/oedema), pneumothorax, lung cancer (haemoptysis/weight loss) — before treating

Treats the exacerbation correctly: increased bronchodilator, oral PREDNISOLONE 30 mg OD for 5 days, and an antibiotic on NICE NG114 judgement (sputum colour change with increased volume, previous exacerbations, complication risk, previous sputum results) — here amoxicillin, doxycycline or clarithromycin for 5 days — not antibiotics reflexively for every flare
Decides disposition (treat at home vs admit) on severity/comorbidity/support, and provides inhaler optimisation and a personalised self-management/rescue-pack plan with clear instructions

Keeps the NICE NG12 LUNG criteria in mind for an ever-smoker aged 40+ — urgent CXR within 2 weeks for 1 or more unexplained symptoms, so a CXR if the exacerbation does not resolve or there is weight loss or appetite loss, and a suspected cancer pathway referral for unexplained haemoptysis — rather than letting repeated rescue packs mask a tumour

Delivers the teachable-moment cessation OFFER well — Very Brief Advice (ask permission, advise plainly, act), offering combination NRT/varenicline/bupropion (or vaping harm-reduction) plus stop-smoking-service referral — addressing fatalism that it is "too late"
Reads the defensiveness as guilt/shame/fatalism, treats the flare competently to earn trust, and makes the cessation offer respectfully WITHOUT colluding with "don’t mention it" or hectoring
Builds rapport with a defensive patient, acknowledges he has heard it before, and checks understanding of the treatment and self-management plan

Safety-nets and follows up: deterioration red flags (worsening breathlessness, drowsiness/confusion, fever, haemoptysis) and when to seek urgent help/admission, review after the exacerbation, CXR/spirometry as indicated, cessation support arranged, and self-management reinforced

worked.txt: "Let’s get you sorted. First a few quick checks so I treat the right thing: are you breathless just moving or at rest too? Any fever, chest pain when you breathe in, calf swelling, or coughing up blood? … None of that, and you’re talking in full sentences on the video — good, that points to a straightforward flare. If anything changes, or I’m unsure, I’ll get you seen in person today so we can listen to your chest."

"Your phlegm’s gone green and there’s more of it, so a course of antibiotics is justified this time, plus the steroid tablets — prednisolone 30 a day for 5 days — and step up your blue inhaler. Let’s make sure your rescue pack and plan are up to date so you can act fast next time."

"One thing because you smoke: if this doesn’t settle, or you ever cough up blood or lose weight, I’ll want a chest X-ray — not to alarm you, just so we never put something more serious down to ‘the usual chest’."

"Can I mention the smoking just once, not to nag — is that okay? … The single biggest thing for your breathing is stopping, and crucially it helps even now, at this stage. I’m not here to judge; I’m here to make it easier if you ever want to."

"If you’re open to it, the things that genuinely work are a combination of nicotine patches and a quick-acting form, or a tablet like varenicline, plus our stop-smoking team who really boost your chances. Switching to vaping is also far less harmful than cigarettes. No pressure — the offer’s there whenever."

"If you get more breathless, drowsy or confused, develop a fever, or cough up blood, that’s urgent — ring us or 999. Let’s review you after this settles to check your inhalers and lung function. And the cessation offer stays open — just say the word."

f.learning: A COPD exacerbation in a smoker must be treated competently AND used as a teachable cessation moment. First GRADE severity and exclude the sinister mimics — pneumonia (fever), PE (pleuritic pain, sudden onset, calf swelling), heart failure (orthopnoea, oedema), pneumothorax (sudden severe breathlessness) and lung cancer (haemoptysis, weight loss) — checking speech, breathing effort and conscious level on video (sats only with a home oximeter), with a same-day face-to-face assessment if in doubt; talking in full sentences with no fever, pain or haemoptysis is reassuring for a straightforward infective flare but the exclusion must be explicit, and admit if severe. Treat correctly: increase the short-acting bronchodilator, give oral PREDNISOLONE 30 mg once daily for 5 days, and decide on an ANTIBIOTIC by NICE NG114 judgement — sputum colour change with increased volume or thickness, previous exacerbations and admissions, complication risk and previous sputum results (here supporting amoxicillin, doxycycline or clarithromycin for 5 days) — not reflexively for every flare — plus inhaler optimisation and a personalised self-management/rescue-pack plan. Keep the NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, last updated April 2026) LUNG criteria in mind: an urgent CXR (within 2 weeks) for anyone aged 40 and over who has ever smoked with 1 or more unexplained symptoms (cough, fatigue, breathlessness, chest pain, weight loss, appetite loss), and a suspected cancer pathway referral for unexplained haemoptysis at 40 and over, and image rather than let repeated rescue packs mask a tumour if a flare does not resolve. The examinable communication is the cessation OFFER done as Very Brief Advice (ask permission, advise plainly that stopping is the single most effective intervention and helps even now, act by offering combination NRT/varenicline/bupropion or vaping harm-reduction plus a stop-smoking-service referral), reading the patient’s defensiveness as guilt/shame/fatalism, earning trust by treating the flare well, and respecting autonomy — neither colluding with "don’t mention it" nor hectoring. Safety-net for deterioration and follow up.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG115 (COPD in over 16s, 2018, updated 2019; reviewed July 2026) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [2] NICE NG114 (COPD exacerbation: antimicrobial prescribing, 2018) · [4] NICE NG209 (tobacco: preventing uptake, promoting quitting, 2021) · [5] NCSCT Very Brief Advice on smoking
knowledge.summary: Grade the flare and exclude its mimics, then treat: more reliever, prednisolone 30 mg for 5 days, and an antibiotic on the NG114 judgement. Use the flare as the moment to offer stop-smoking help, briefly and without a lecture.

points.t: Breathlessness at rest, speech, drowsiness or confusion, cyanosis, and oxygen saturation if it can be measured. Exclude pneumonia (fever, focal signs), PE (sudden onset, pleuritic pain, calf swelling), heart failure (orthopnoea, oedema) and pneumothorax (sudden severe breathlessness). NICE NG115 [1] lists factors favouring hospital treatment, including severe breathlessness, confusion, cyanosis, poor general condition and poor social support.

NICE NG115 [1]: oral prednisolone 30 mg once daily for 5 days for an exacerbation with a significant increase in breathlessness that interferes with daily activities. Warn about sleep, mood and blood glucose effects.

NICE NG114 [2]: weigh severity (sputum colour change with increased volume or thickness), previous exacerbations and admissions, risk of complications, previous sputum results and resistance risk. First choices are amoxicillin, doxycycline or clarithromycin, for 5 days (doses per BNF). His purulent, increased sputum supports an antibiotic this time.

NICE NG115 [1]: offer a rescue pack of steroid and antibiotic to people who have had an exacerbation in the last year, understand when to use it and are confident to do so, with an instruction to tell the practice each time it is used. Frequent use is a trigger for review, not just re-supply.

NICE NG12 [3]: urgent chest X-ray within 2 weeks for people aged 40 and over who have ever smoked with 1 or more unexplained symptoms (cough, fatigue, breathlessness, chest pain, weight loss, appetite loss); suspected cancer pathway referral for unexplained haemoptysis at 40 and over. A flare that does not settle, or any haemoptysis or weight loss, needs imaging.

NCSCT [5]: Ask, Advise, Act in under a minute. NICE NG209 [4]: offer behavioural support with varenicline, cytisinicline (cytisine), combination NRT or nicotine-containing e-cigarettes; refer to a stop-smoking service. NICE NG115 [1]: helping people with COPD who smoke to stop is one of the most important parts of their care, at every stage.
Review once settled: inhaler technique and treatment step, rescue-pack plan, vaccinations and pulmonary rehabilitation if functionally limited (NICE NG115 [1]).

dg.d: Open start; acknowledged his request and his “no lecture” request before structuring.
Impact on daily activity, support at home, and smoking, raised only with permission.
Oxygen saturation and chest examination today; chest X-ray if not settling or red flags; allergy check before antibiotic.
Infective exacerbation versus pneumonia, PE, heart failure, pneumothorax and lung cancer.
Asked about fever, pleuritic pain, calf swelling, haemoptysis, weight loss, drowsiness and breathlessness at rest.
Named an infective COPD exacerbation and explained why an antibiotic is justified this time.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Prednisolone 30 mg for 5 days, 5-day NG114 antibiotic, increased reliever; Very Brief Advice with a real offer.
Smoking cessation offer (varenicline, combination NRT, vape, service); rescue-pack plan and vaccinations at review.
999 and same-day triggers named; review booked; chest X-ray if non-resolving.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options

Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up the fatalism (“too late”, “only thing I enjoy”) and answered it.
Idea (usual chest flare), concern (being lectured), expectation (usual rescue course).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — guilt and fatalism about smoking ("too late now"); tired of being lectured; quietly worried about not being around for his grandchildren — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Morning Frank, Dr Singh here. Sounds like your chest is playing up. Tell me how it’s been.
More puffed than usual, coughing more, phlegm’s gone green. I know the drill — steroids and antibiotics like last time. And please don’t start on about the smoking.
Understood. Let’s get your chest sorted first. I need a few quick questions so I’m treating the right thing, then we’ll agree the plan. Okay?
model.why: Acknowledges his request and sets a clear structure

model.text: Go on then.
How long has this been going on, and how breathless are you now — just walking about, or sitting still too?
Four days. Worse walking. I’m alright sitting.
You’re talking to me in full sentences, which is good. Any fever or shivers?
model.why: Screens for pneumonia and notes speech

model.text: No.
Any sharp pain in the chest when you breathe in, a sudden change in your breathing, or a swollen, painful calf?
None of that.
Any coughing up blood, or weight dropping off without trying?
model.why: Screens NICE NG12 lung red flags

model.text: No blood. Not that I’ve noticed with the weight.
Ankles swelling, or needing extra pillows to breathe at night? And any drowsiness or muddled thinking?
model.why: Screens for heart failure and CO2 retention

model.text: No, no.
And how much more phlegm is there, as well as the colour?
Loads more. Thick and green.
What do you think is going on this time?
Same as always. My chest. It’s what happens.
And you’re hoping for the usual course. Is anything worrying you about it?
Just want it sorted. And not the lecture.

From what you’ve told me this sounds like a flare of your COPD from a chest infection, and nothing points to pneumonia, a clot or your heart. Because your phlegm has changed colour and there’s much more of it, an antibiotic is the right call this time, along with steroid tablets.
model.why: Shares a working diagnosis and a reasoned antibiotic decision

model.text: Told you.

You did. So: prednisolone 30 milligrams once a day for five days, and a five-day antibiotic — I’ll check your allergy record before I choose it. Use your blue inhaler more often as you need it. I’d also like someone to check your oxygen level and listen to your chest today if you can come in.
model.why: Correct NG115/NG114 treatment and a face-to-face check

model.text: I can pop in.
Can I mention the smoking just once? I promise I’ll keep it short, and it’s your call.
model.why: Asks permission — the first step of Very Brief Advice

model.text: Go on. You will anyway.

I won’t lecture. The one thing that changes how your lungs do from here is stopping, and it helps even at this stage. The best way to do it is with stop-smoking support plus a treatment — patches with a quick-acting nicotine product, a tablet called varenicline, or a vape. That roughly triples your chances compared with willpower alone.
model.why: Advise and Act: states benefit and offers evidence-based help

model.text: It’s too late now. And it’s the only thing I enjoy.

That’s honest, and I hear it. It’s not too late — your lungs would lose function more slowly from the day you stop. And a vape could keep some of what you enjoy without the smoke. I’m not asking you to decide now. Can I send you the stop-smoking service details so they’re there when you want them?
model.why: Addresses fatalism with respect and leaves the offer open

model.text: Send them. No promises.
That’s fair. I’d also like to see you once you’ve recovered to check your inhalers, your rescue-pack plan and your jabs.

If you get breathless sitting still, can’t finish a sentence, become drowsy or confused, or your lips go blue, call 999. If you get a fever, cough up blood, or you’re not improving in a couple of days, contact us the same day.
model.why: Specific red flags and time frame

model.text: Right.
And if this doesn’t settle, I’ll arrange a chest X-ray — because you smoke, I never want to put something else down to your usual chest. Can you tell me back the plan?
Steroids five days, antibiotic, more blue inhaler, pop in today, 999 if I can’t talk or get drowsy, X-ray if it doesn’t clear.
Perfect. The nurse will see you later, and I’ll book your review.

social.t: For many long-term smokers, smoking is pleasure, routine and stress relief. Fatalism (“too late”) and shame drive defensiveness; respect it and leave the offer open.
Poor social support is one of the NICE NG115 factors favouring hospital treatment of an exacerbation.

legal.t: If his work is affected, a fit note may be needed during the flare; he can self-certify for the first 7 days.

professional.t: NICE NG114: document why an antibiotic was or was not given. Reflex antibiotics for every flare drive resistance.
GMC Decision making and consent (2020): give balanced information and respect his choice about smoking without withdrawing care.

community.t: Local NHS stop-smoking service, community pharmacy stop-smoking support, and the NHS Quit Smoking app.

redFlags: Breathlessness at rest, unable to complete sentences, cyanosis
Fever or pleuritic pain (pneumonia), sudden onset or calf swelling (PE)
Haemoptysis or weight loss in a smoker
psychosocial: Support at home and ability to manage
Smoking: pleasure, habit, previous attempts — with permission
ice: Idea: “It’s my chest again, same as always.”
Expectation: the usual steroid and antibiotic

playbook.diagnosis: “This is a flare of your COPD, most likely from a chest infection. Nothing you’ve told me suggests pneumonia, a clot or your heart, and because your phlegm has changed and increased, an antibiotic is right this time.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your airways are like narrowed pipes. An infection makes the lining swell and fill with phlegm, so the steroid calms the swelling and the antibiotic tackles the infection.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked me not to lecture you, and I won’t. I’ll mention the smoking once, and it’s your call.”
management.psychosocial: Very Brief Advice with permission; answer the fatalism with a specific benefit; offer a vape as harm reduction; leave the service details with him.
sharedPlan: Prednisolone 30 mg once daily for 5 days; 5-day antibiotic per NG114 (amoxicillin, doxycycline or clarithromycin; dose per BNF); more reliever
Face-to-face oxygen saturation and chest check today
Post-flare review: inhalers, rescue-pack plan, vaccines, pulmonary rehabilitation if limited; cessation offer open
safetyNet: 999: breathless at rest, cannot finish sentences, drowsy or confused, blue lips
Same day: fever, haemoptysis, or not improving in 2 days; chest X-ray if not settling

pitfalls.intro: This station tests two things at once: safe flare management and a smoking conversation that is neither avoided nor preached. Most candidates get one right and lose the other.

items.fail: Handing over the rescue course with no severity or exclusion questions because he “knows the drill”.
items.why: “Fails to exclude serious alternatives.” Pneumonia, PE and heart failure can all present as “my chest again”.
items.fix: Sixty seconds of targeted questions, said aloud: “so I’m treating the right thing.”

items.fail: Prednisolone 40 mg for 7 to 14 days, or antibiotics for 7 days by habit.
items.why: NICE NG115 says 30 mg for 5 days; NICE NG114 says 5 days of antibiotic.
items.fix: State the dose and duration plainly: “30 milligrams once a day for five days.”

items.fail: Colluding — never mentioning smoking because he asked you not to.
items.why: Missing the teachable moment loses Tasks marks; examiners expect Very Brief Advice.
items.fix: Ask permission: “Can I mention it once, briefly?” Then advise and offer.

items.fail: Lecturing: listing smoking harms and telling him he must stop.
items.why: “Does not respect the patient’s autonomy.” Defensiveness hardens and the offer is lost.
items.fix: One benefit, one offer, then leave the door open.

items.fail: No chest X-ray plan for a 40-pack-year smoker whose flares keep recurring.
items.why: NICE NG12 sets a low threshold for ever-smokers aged 40 and over.
items.fix: “If this doesn’t settle, or you cough up blood or lose weight, I’ll arrange an X-ray.”

items.fail: “Come back if you’re worse” as the only safety-net.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing feedback statement.
items.fix: Name the 999 signs and the same-day signs, give a time frame, and book the review.

avoid.instead: “Can I mention the smoking just once, briefly? It’s your call.”
avoid.why: Permission turns a lecture into an offer and keeps him listening.

Steroids five days, antibiotic, more blue inhaler, pop in today, 999 if I can’t talk or get drowsy, X-ray if it doesn’t clear.
Perfect. The nurse will see you later, and I’ll book your review.

SCA_STEM.name: Frank Dolan
meds: COPD inhalers as on the repeat list, including a short-acting reliever
Previous rescue courses of steroid and antibiotic
SCA_STEM.recent: Four days of more breathlessness, more cough and green sputum. No fever, pleuritic pain or haemoptysis reported.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation: “I just need the steroids and antibiotics I usually get.”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE NG115 (COPD in over 16s, 2018, updated 2019; reviewed July 2026) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [2] NICE NG114 (COPD exacerbation: antimicrobial prescribing, 2018) · [4] NICE NG209 (tobacco: preventing uptake, promoting quitting, 2021) · [5] NCSCT Very Brief Advice on smoking
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Grade the flare and exclude its mimics, then treat: more reliever, prednisolone 30 mg for 5 days, and an antibiotic on the NG114 judgement. Use the flare as the moment to offer stop-smoking help, briefly and without a lecture.

points.t: Breathlessness at rest, speech, drowsiness or confusion, cyanosis, and oxygen saturation if it can be measured. Exclude pneumonia (fever, focal signs), PE (sudden onset, pleuritic pain, calf swelling), heart failure (orthopnoea, oedema) and pneumothorax (sudden severe breathlessness). NICE NG115 [1] lists factors favouring hospital treatment, including severe breathlessness, confusion, cyanosis, poor general condition and poor social support.

NICE NG115 [1]: oral prednisolone 30 mg once daily for 5 days for an exacerbation with a significant increase in breathlessness that interferes with daily activities. Warn about sleep, mood and blood glucose effects.

NICE NG114 [2]: weigh severity (sputum colour change with increased volume or thickness), previous exacerbations and admissions, risk of complications, previous sputum results and resistance risk. First choices are amoxicillin, doxycycline or clarithromycin, for 5 days (doses per BNF). His purulent, increased sputum supports an antibiotic this time.

NICE NG115 [1]: offer a rescue pack of steroid and antibiotic to people who have had an exacerbation in the last year, understand when to use it and are confident to do so, with an instruction to tell the practice each time it is used. Frequent use is a trigger for review, not just re-supply.

NICE NG12 [3]: urgent chest X-ray within 2 weeks for people aged 40 and over who have ever smoked with 1 or more unexplained symptoms (cough, fatigue, breathlessness, chest pain, weight loss, appetite loss); suspected cancer pathway referral for unexplained haemoptysis at 40 and over. A flare that does not settle, or any haemoptysis or weight loss, needs imaging.

NCSCT [5]: Ask, Advise, Act in under a minute. NICE NG209 [4]: offer behavioural support with varenicline, cytisinicline (cytisine), combination NRT or nicotine-containing e-cigarettes; refer to a stop-smoking service. NICE NG115 [1]: helping people with COPD who smoke to stop is one of the most important parts of their care, at every stage.
Review once settled: inhaler technique and treatment step, rescue-pack plan, vaccinations and pulmonary rehabilitation if functionally limited (NICE NG115 [1]).

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open start; acknowledged his request and his “no lecture” request before structuring.
Impact on daily activity, support at home, and smoking, raised only with permission.
Picked up the fatalism (“too late”, “only thing I enjoy”) and answered it.
Idea (usual chest flare), concern (being lectured), expectation (usual rescue course).
Oxygen saturation and chest examination today; chest X-ray if not settling or red flags; allergy check before antibiotic.
Infective exacerbation versus pneumonia, PE, heart failure, pneumothorax and lung cancer.
Asked about fever, pleuritic pain, calf swelling, haemoptysis, weight loss, drowsiness and breathlessness at rest.
Named an infective COPD exacerbation and explained why an antibiotic is justified this time.
Prednisolone 30 mg for 5 days, 5-day NG114 antibiotic, increased reliever; Very Brief Advice with a real offer.
Smoking cessation offer (varenicline, combination NRT, vape, service); rescue-pack plan and vaccinations at review.
999 and same-day triggers named; review booked; chest X-ray if non-resolving.

social.t: For many long-term smokers, smoking is pleasure, routine and stress relief. Fatalism (“too late”) and shame drive defensiveness; respect it and leave the offer open.
Poor social support is one of the NICE NG115 factors favouring hospital treatment of an exacerbation.

legal.t: If his work is affected, a fit note may be needed during the flare; he can self-certify for the first 7 days.

professional.t: NICE NG114: document why an antibiotic was or was not given. Reflex antibiotics for every flare drive resistance.
GMC Decision making and consent (2020): give balanced information and respect his choice about smoking without withdrawing care.

community.t: Local NHS stop-smoking service, community pharmacy stop-smoking support, and the NHS Quit Smoking app.

redFlags: Breathlessness at rest, unable to complete sentences, cyanosis
Fever or pleuritic pain (pneumonia), sudden onset or calf swelling (PE)
Haemoptysis or weight loss in a smoker
psychosocial: Support at home and ability to manage
Smoking: pleasure, habit, previous attempts — with permission
ice: Idea: “It’s my chest again, same as always.”
Expectation: the usual steroid and antibiotic

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is a flare of your COPD, most likely from a chest infection. Nothing you’ve told me suggests pneumonia, a clot or your heart, and because your phlegm has changed and increased, an antibiotic is right this time.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your airways are like narrowed pipes. An infection makes the lining swell and fill with phlegm, so the steroid calms the swelling and the antibiotic tackles the infection.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked me not to lecture you, and I won’t. I’ll mention the smoking once, and it’s your call.”
management.psychosocial: Very Brief Advice with permission; answer the fatalism with a specific benefit; offer a vape as harm reduction; leave the service details with him.
sharedPlan: Prednisolone 30 mg once daily for 5 days; 5-day antibiotic per NG114 (amoxicillin, doxycycline or clarithromycin; dose per BNF); more reliever
Face-to-face oxygen saturation and chest check today
Post-flare review: inhalers, rescue-pack plan, vaccines, pulmonary rehabilitation if limited; cessation offer open
safetyNet: 999: breathless at rest, cannot finish sentences, drowsy or confused, blue lips
Same day: fever, haemoptysis, or not improving in 2 days; chest X-ray if not settling

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests two things at once: safe flare management and a smoking conversation that is neither avoided nor preached. Most candidates get one right and lose the other.

items.fail: Handing over the rescue course with no severity or exclusion questions because he “knows the drill”.
items.why: “Fails to exclude serious alternatives.” Pneumonia, PE and heart failure can all present as “my chest again”.
items.fix: Sixty seconds of targeted questions, said aloud: “so I’m treating the right thing.”

items.fail: Prednisolone 40 mg for 7 to 14 days, or antibiotics for 7 days by habit.
items.why: NICE NG115 says 30 mg for 5 days; NICE NG114 says 5 days of antibiotic.
items.fix: State the dose and duration plainly: “30 milligrams once a day for five days.”

items.fail: Colluding — never mentioning smoking because he asked you not to.
items.why: Missing the teachable moment loses Tasks marks; examiners expect Very Brief Advice.
items.fix: Ask permission: “Can I mention it once, briefly?” Then advise and offer.

items.fail: Lecturing: listing smoking harms and telling him he must stop.
items.why: “Does not respect the patient’s autonomy.” Defensiveness hardens and the offer is lost.
items.fix: One benefit, one offer, then leave the door open.

items.fail: No chest X-ray plan for a 40-pack-year smoker whose flares keep recurring.
items.why: NICE NG12 sets a low threshold for ever-smokers aged 40 and over.
items.fix: “If this doesn’t settle, or you cough up blood or lose weight, I’ll arrange an X-ray.”

items.fail: “Come back if you’re worse” as the only safety-net.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing feedback statement.
items.fix: Name the 999 signs and the same-day signs, give a time frame, and book the review.
